title: Lit From Behind, A Roman Cup Turns Blood Red

segments.narration: Light from behind turns this Roman cup blood red. In daylight the same glass is jade green. One object, two colours.
It was carved in the fourth century, probably around 290 to 325 AD, from a single block of glass, then cut away.
So how does one cup hold two colours? Nobody could explain it for centuries, and it is the only complete Roman piece like it.
In 1990 researchers put fragments under a microscope. The glass is salted with gold and silver particles about seventy nanometres across.
Those specks scatter and absorb light differently depending on where it comes from. Roman glassmakers likely stumbled onto it by accident, and never fully controlled it.

verdicts.claim: In 1990 researchers examining fragments under a microscope found gold and silver particles about seventy nanometres across dispersed in the glass.
verdicts.note: Smithsonian reports that in 1990 researchers in England examined broken fragments under a microscope and found the metal particles. The sources disagree on size: Wikipedia says about 70 nanometres, Smithsonian about 50. The narration uses 70 and says 'about'.

verdicts.claim: The colour shift is caused by the way those metal particles scatter and absorb light, and the makers probably did not understand or control the process.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia attributes the effect to surface plasmon resonance, with the fine particles scattering blue more than red in transmitted light, and says the process remains unclear and was probably not well understood or controlled by its makers, likely found through accidental contamination. Smithsonian argues the opposite, that the precise mixture shows deliberate skill; the narration follows the cautious reading and says 'likely'.
